content.title: Response
content.comment:
**- Is ML necessary for creating compilation/parsing errors?**

Yes. Program errors created by manually designed heuristics are known to be different from realistics errors. This distribution mismatch exists for both VarMisuse (He et al., 2022) and compilation/parsing errors (Yasunaga & Liang, 2021). To address this issue, BIFI (Yasunaga & Liang, 2021) uses ML to create compilation/parsing errors, which are more realistic than errors created by manual heuristics and lead to better ML-based bug fixers. BreaC (this work) even outperforms BIFI.

**- Does BreaC outperforms heuristics?**

Yes. The paper compares two times with DrRepair (Yasunaga & Liang, 2020), which creates non-compilable code using heuristics designed by human experts to train bug fixers. First, in Table 3, the paper shows that BreaC outperforms BIFI (Yasunaga & Liang, 2021), a follow-up work of DrRepair. This immediately means that BreaC outperforms DrRepair (fix accuracy 76.3 vs 66.1 on DeepFix). Second, in section 4.3, paragraph “Superiority over Synthetic Errors”, the paper shows that the erroneous programs generated by BreaC have 44% lower perplexity than those generated by the heuristics of DrRepair.

**- Are the technical aspects of the paper necessary, especially training phase II?**

Yes, the ablation study in Table 4 clearly shows that our technical components are all important.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper describes BreaC, a class-conditional language model (CCLM) that can generate C++ programs that are compilable or uncompilable, controlled by the class input good | bad. One of the motivations for BreaC is to demonstrate attacks on LLMs for program synthesis, to cause the models to generate bad (uncompilable) programs. To train BreaC, the authors used conditional maximum likelihood and unlikelihood (CMLU) and a self-adversarial reinforcement learning (RL) process that are arranged in two-phrase approach. The authors demonstrated that BreaC could successfully model both good and bad after the two phase training, and that the bad examples it generates fail compilation with a high likelihood. In addition, the authors showed that the trained BreaC model can attack another LLM effectively through the GeDi paradigm and cause the LLM to show a significant decrease in the rate of compilable code.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Main strengths:

1. Innovative formulation of breaking code generation as a self-adversarial RL problem, and combination with the CMLU loss function.

2. Extensive ablation study on the model to demonstrate the relative contribution of different parts of the overall design to the final outcome.

Weaknesses

1. From reading the manuscript, it is unclear to me whether the attack requirement is realistic. Under what circumstances would the attack have read and write access to the next-token logits of the attacked LLM? It seems that most 3rd party users of a program synthesizer as a service would only be able to read the generated tokens, and would not have read, leaving alone write, access to such a model. The authors should provide more background and justification for exploring such an attack requirement.

2. This paper lacks a comparison against a non-ML and less computationally-costly baseline for generating uncompilable code. The examples shown in Figure 3, which are bad programs generated by the trained BreaC model, are trivial changes involving short edits such as deleting a curly brace or a type word ("int"). It seems that a heuristic-based non-ML algorithm can be written to take the abstract syntax tree (AST) of a good program, and mutate it slightly in this fashion. Then the output of this non-ML algorithm can be evaluate in its perplexity (degree of being realistic) and rate of being bad. This would have formed a convincing baseline for demonstrating the added value of the LLM-based BreaC model.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Apart from the lack of a clear motivation for the attack scenario I described above, this paper is well-written and easy to follow. It cites related literature properly. The work is original in several aspects, but the original ideas are unfortunately not sufficiently justified through comparison with a meaningful non-ML baseline.
content.summary_of_the_review: To summarize, this paper contains some interesting and innovative ideas about generating code examples that are compilable. But it lacks sufficient motivation for the underlying question (adversarial attack of a program-synthesis LLM with a peculiar attack requirement) and comparison against a meaningful baseline.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to train a class-conditional language model (CCLM) that can generate code with compilation and parsing errors. The proposed approach, BreaC, uses unlikelihood training and adversarial reinforcement learning. The paper presents experimental results in two settings, (1) adversarial and (2) benign. In the adversarial scenario, Breac reduces the compilation rate of LLMs. The paper shows that CodeGen-350M CCLM breaks CodeGen-2.7B LM and reduces the top-1 compilation rate from 80.6% to 4.5%.  In the benign scenario, BreaC can produce realistic erroneous programs that allow the construction of parallel bug-fixing training datasets. The paper shows such a dataset is used to train fixers to reduce the failure rate of BIFI by 16% on the DeepFix dataset and 36% on the Github-Python dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
__Strength__
- The motivation for training a mode to break LLM-based code generators is sound.
- The use of unlikelihood training to train a model to differentiate between correct and erroneous programs is interesting. Combining this with reinforcement learning (as self-adversarial learning), the proposed approach generalizes well by leveraging sequence-level learning.
- Strong empirical performance.
- Overall, the paper is well written.

__Weaknesses__
- The key components of the proposed method exist in prior works.
- The attack scenarios explained are not well motivated.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
__Clarity and Quality__
- The paper is overall well written.
- Evaluation of code completion tasks would be a big plus.

__Novelty__

Although the key components of the proposed method exist in prior works, their use in this work is well thought out.

__Reproducibility__

The proposed method uses a complicated training scheme. Therefore, the release of source code would be crucial for reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall the paper makes a significant contribution by presenting strong empirical results on relevant tasks. However, I am concerned about the attack settings considered in this work.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper presents BreaC, a method for breaking LLMs of code, by making them generate erroneous code. 
The approach is evaluated on the task of generating code with compilation and parsing errors. This can allow creating parallel (erroneous,fixed) example pairs, to train other, downstream, bug fixing models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Weaknesses
* **Motivation** - The main task is generating $(erroneous,fixed)$ program example pairs. I could not really understand the motivation for generating erroneous code. The introduction states that:
> An ignored but critical direction is the attack perspective, which can expose limitations, facilitate interpretation, provide adversarial examples, and benefit the training of robust models

but does not really explain why would one want to generate erroneous code? "expose limitations, facilitate interpretation, provide adversarial examples, and benefit the training of robust models" are vague reasons that either were not explained, or not empirically evaluated. I was not convinced that this task is really meaningful/useful.

This task might be important if the resulting pairs lead to training much better code fixers, but the code fixing task was evaluated as a secondary task with only a single baseline.

* The kind of errors that BreaC creates are only parsing and compilation errors:
> BreaC significantly reduces the compilation rate of a variety of LLMs

Do we really need a machine learning model to break compilation/parsing? Figure 1 shows an example, where the model added an unnecessary `)` character. Do we really need a machine learning model to add/remove colons and parentheses?

Figure 3 shows additional examples, where the generated erroneous programs have an extra `}` character; an ` + endl` was added to a floating point calculation, which is obviously incorrect; or that an undeclared variable was used.
I do not understand why are these examples challenging, as these are easy to create and easy to detect.

I do understand the difficulty in finding and creating VarMisuse errors, for example, as in Allamanis et al., 2018 ("Learning to Represent Programs with Graphs") or Yefet et al (2020), where humans and models would not necessarily notice the error.
Further, training on such hard-to-notice examples may lead to stronger and more robust downstream bug fixers.
But why do the examples in Figure 1 and Figure 3 help a bug-fixing model train better? They seem to be very easy to detect and fix.

* **Unrealistic**  - the approach perturbed the next-token probabilities of the model under attack. In which real-world scenario is this attack realistic? Classic work on adversarial examples such as Szegedy et al (2014) attacked the model by providing adversarial *input*, which is an attack surface that is typically open to the user of a machine learning model. But in which cases does a user have access to the next-token probabilities? Why is it a challenge to break the prediction if the attacker has access to the output probabilities? Is this attack meant to be realistic on its own, or just as an intrinsic objective for downstream bug fixing?

* **Technical complexity** - the proposed approach requires an additional model, that involves two stages of training: unlikelihood training, and an RL training stage. I see it as a disadvantage, since I was not convinced that the difficulty of the task justifies the technical complexity.

* **Evaluation** - 
    * The evaluation applies the proposed approach on many models, but I was not convinced that there aren't simpler approaches. Since the task seems relatively simple, can't simple heuristics result in similar results? For example:
        * To break programs syntactically, we can inject random colons and parentheses, where their probability is higher than in other locations.
        * Fixing unparsable programs can be usually performed easily by the parser.
    * Table 3 looks like the only realistic downstream task (bug fixing), but BreaC is compared only to a single baseline of BIFI, but not to other recent bug fixers such as:
        * "Self-Supervised Bug Detection and Repair" - Allamanis et al., 2021
        * "TFix: Learning to Fix Coding Errors with a Text-to-Text Transformer" - Berabi et al., 2021.
        * "Studying the Usage of Text-To-Text Transfer Transformer to Support Code-Related Tasks" - Mastropaolo et al., 2021

## Additional Questions
1. Section 2 says that:
> We say a program $x$ is good if $x$ can be compiled or parsed

- what if it can be parsed, but not compiled? Is it "good" or "bad"?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity
Most of the paper is clear, although I could not really understand training phase 2, and why it is needed.

### Novelty and originality
Technically, the approach is very close to GeDi (Krause et al., 2021). 
In many places in the paper, the proposed approach is even presented as GeDi.
What is the novelty compared to GeDi?
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed approach is interesting, but I was not convinced that the tasks are realistic and helpful, and that the technical complexity is justified. Thus, I vote for rejection, but I would love to read the authors' response.

content.title: Breaking Large Language Model-based Code Generation
content.abstract: We propose BreaC, a new method for attacking large language models (LLMs) to excessively generate erroneous code. BreaC works by training a class-conditional language model (CCLM) that conditions code generation on a binary attribute specifying whether the output code should contain errors. The CCLM is not only able to generate erroneous programs but can also control other, much larger LLMs to do so without access to their weights. The training of the CCLM leverages unlikelihood training, as well as reinforcement learning that treats the two generation branches of the CCLM as adversaries. We instantiate BreaC on the task of generating code with compilation and parsing errors. Our extensive evaluation demonstrates that BreaC is effective in both adversarial and benign scenarios. For the adversarial scenario, BreaC greatly reduces the compilation rate of various LLMs while maintaining the perplexity of generated programs. For the benign scenario, BreaC is able to produce realistic erroneous programs from correct programs, enabling one to construct parallel training datasets. We demonstrate the high utility of these datasets by training neural bug fixers that significantly surpass the state-of-the-art.
